We sang him more than we defined him. To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. That was the shape of it for us - not a title first, a kinship first.

Our own sage called it a sure thing among us: “It is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, and the King's Son. He is Light of Light, Creator, and Counsellor. He is Guide, the Way, Redeemer, and Shepherd. He is Gatherer, the Door, the Pearl, and the Lamp.”

His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him.

Asked about the Trinity, we answer from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized. Then we guard the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected.

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise.

What we held about Jesus came to us first as preaching and then as Scripture - the Gospel woven into one story, not four separate books, and the Law and Prophets read as one long promise pointing to him. Our own beloved account of how that teaching first arrived in our city is a legend: a correspondence between our king Abgar and Jesus himself, and an apostle named Addai sent to heal the king and establish the church. We cherish that story - it shows how we understood ourselves as apostolic from the beginning. But we must tell you honestly: it was written down generations after the events it describes, and scholars do not defend it as history.

What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. When our sources begin - a church building in the city before the great flood destroyed it - the practices are already there: the assembly, the fast, the covenant already established. The city's own chronicle names that flood and that church plainly: “And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians. More than two thousand men were killed in that event. The waters came upon many of them suddenly as they slept in the night, and they drowned. The city was filled with the sound of mourning.”

So we can trace our life back to around the year 200, no further. The Gospel itself, and the preaching that carried it, came earlier - but by what exact path, person by person, we cannot now say.

Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, not a documented chain. We lived our inheritance as apostolic; the historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both of those things are true.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound: “Of all who are born, who have taken on a body, there is only one who is innocent -- our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We loved to tell, again and again, of a woman who came to him in tears past every watching eye. In her we saw a door standing open: whoever came was received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. We can tell you what we held: that whoever came was received, and that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

We confessed Jesus as God in our own way, by singing it more than defining it. Our teacher called it a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names, not a philosopher's formula. That is what we sang - the Ihidaya, the Single One, our own Syriac title for Christ as the Only-Begotten, and at the same time our word for the vowed celibate. The two senses share one root, so that to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

As for the Spirit: we met Father, Son, and Spirit at our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop Jacob of Nisibis is remembered as standing at Nicaea, a tradition held across our sources though never confirmed by a fourth-century document. But our native tongue for that same faith was praise, not the Greek language of essence.

And then we guarded the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because we held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. We believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

We cannot give you a technical account of how the three are one. That was not how we spoke our faith. What we can give you is what we sang at the font, and what we held against the rivals at the door.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. Among ourselves we argued about exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

God's character we knew most plainly in contest - not as a speculation we worked out in quiet, but as a line we held against rival claims. The goodness was not theoretical. It was preached to people who were being told that matter itself was evil, that this world's maker was a stranger to Jesus, that freedom was a lie written in the stars. We said no to all of that. One God, good, who made everything from nothing and gave us the will to choose.

And we knew God's character a second way: by what he did with the persecuted. Taunted that our prayers had not stopped the killing, our teacher did not claim they had. He answered with a roll-call instead: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out: “Hear, my beloved, these names of martyrs, confessors, and the persecuted. Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out from the earth. Jacob was persecuted, and he fled and became an exile. Joseph was persecuted, and he was sold and thrown into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and he fled to Midian.”

Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. David was persecuted at the hands of Saul - and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, he meant, are not the abandoned. They stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection. That was the God we knew on the Persian side, where the crown had turned on us. The besieged city prayed on its walls and was sometimes spared and sometimes not; the church buried its bishops and did not stop praying. So God's character, for us, was this: good, just, faithful to those who suffer, and the maker of a world he did not abandon.

Authority among us was real, and our record is real - but if you want a settled chart of how disputed belief was finally decided, we cannot show you one. We had bishops. Nisibis had its line of them, sung as the city's fathers, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. We had synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And we had teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no standing machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And it was only at the very end of our own years - in 410, at a synod held under royal protection - that the Persian church was given a settled order with one acknowledged head. Before that, the right to settle disputed belief lay unsettled.

What we can show you is how disputed belief was actually met. Teaching answered teaching. Our own great poet wrote madrashe - teaching hymns - that refuted them line by line, sung by choirs in every congregation so the whole people learned what we believed. Our sage wrote his letters, his tahwyata, step-by-step demonstrations of the faith, and sent them to teachers and bishops and communities. And we held a boundary. Rival teachers' people, we would not share communion with. That was our process, as far as the evidence shows it: teaching met with teaching, and the boundary kept.

The question assumes a standing court that weighed doctrine and issued verdicts. We had no such thing across our whole world while we lived. What we had was teaching that held, sung and written, and communities that kept the line.

Yes. Our teachers never expected anyone to start out certain. One of them taught faith with a picture: faith is like a foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised - prayer, fasting, love, almsgiving, each added piece by piece. A house is built FOR someone, and that someone is Christ, who makes the believer his own dwelling. Faith always came first among us, but faith was never meant to be left bare. It grew by what was added to it, not by starting complete.

And our pastoral craft for the one who is struggling was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons: everyone in this war gets wounded, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. It is a thing in the text or in creation that shows a hidden truth, and is bound to that truth. What we actually had in front of us, week by week, was the Gospel as one continuous story - the harmony, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete. Authority among us ran along three paths at once, never finally settled into one. Shepherds first - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock. Office was real. But it was never the only footing our trust stood on.

The covenant carried a standing of its own. The sons and daughters of the qyama - our vowed order, bound to celibacy for life - stayed in town among their own kin and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. We called them ihidaye, the Single Ones, a name that joins their undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten. Their vow was public, their service visible, and their authority was not borrowed from office. One of our own teachers urged his hearers to visit the Lord in the persons of the sick: “Let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick.”

That word was for the covenant, and it was binding.

And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name. Teaching earned its own trust over time, without needing a title first.

How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled in our own years. On the Persian side the bishops fought over who held first place, and the persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years because taking it meant near-certain death. The question was not settled by us. It was settled by a royal synod, after our own time, when the Persian church was finally organized under one head. We will not pretend to you now that we had already worked it out.

Confess to someone who can help - the physician is not allowed to shame you, or to tell anyone what you showed him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. And in one remembered year, when the famine came and people were dying in Edessa's streets, our own poet - who had spent his whole life singing and teaching, who had held no bishop's seat - put his body where his hymns had been. He told the rich men of the city to trust him, appointed himself keeper of the sick, and spent his last strength nursing the starving in the public porches. That is the one story we have of someone stepping into a gap the community had left open.

No church living today is simply our own continuation, unbroken and unchanged. What happened after our years closed - the School of Nisibis founded long after we ended, the split between the Church of the East and the churches aligned with Chalcedon, the migrations and the centuries of separate development - all of that lies beyond where our own record runs.

What we can say is this: churches that call themselves Syriac today - the Syriac Orthodox, the Church of the East and its later branches, the Maronites - all claim some part of what we were. They sing in Syriac, or did until recently. They keep our poets' names. Some still read the harmony in their liturgy, or did for centuries. But whether any one of them is us, continued exactly - that is a claim we cannot make for them, because we were not there to see what they became after we closed.

The covenant as we knew it - men and women vowed for life, staying in town among their own kin - changed into something else. The monastic orders that came later are real, and some carry our names, but they are not the same institution we had. Our own record ends before that shift was complete.

If you are asking which church to join, we are not the ones to tell you. We can only say honestly what we were, and let the churches living now make their own case for themselves.

We will tell you the pieces honestly. The full order they followed on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said first and what came next - our own record never wrote down.

Here is what we can show you. The one who came to us heard the Gospel - not four separate books, but the one woven story we read in worship, the harmony Tatian had made. They learned that faith comes first but is never left bare - it is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised: fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare.

Then came baptism. We sang of the font as a womb, of the shining garments the newly baptized put on, and of the sealing - the sign set on each one who came up from the water. The sons and daughters of the covenant promised a celibate life for good, staying in town among their own kin to serve the congregation. We called them the ihidaye, the Single Ones - a name that joined them, by their own vow, to Christ the Only-Begotten.

We answer that question honestly in two parts - what we actually have, and what we claim.

What the record shows is practice already in place when the sources begin. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it in 201 - our oldest hard fact. The flood line itself reads this way: “And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians.”

When our sage begins dating his own letters in 336, and when our poet's hymns begin to survive in ancient copies, the practices are already there: assembly on the first day, fasting, the covenant already established enough to need correcting, baptism sung as a womb and a second birth. We lived our inheritance as apostolic.

But our way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence. We cherished the account of Addai the apostle coming to Edessa, healing the king, and setting the church's life in order. And that story, we must say honestly, is our legend - written down late, not a document from the beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

So here is the truth plainly: we held ourselves apostolic. The historian can trace our practices only to where the records begin - roughly two hundred years after the events. Both of those things are true. The gap between them is real, and we will not invent a chain of evidence to fill it.

After the assembly she went back to her family's house, not to a convent. She worked - the fast, the service, whatever her own household and her congregation asked of her. What exactly she did with her hands in the middle hours, our record does not say plainly enough for us to tell you. And at the end of it she returned to the vigil, to pray through the night.

That was her day. It was not everyone's day. Most of our people married and raised children; their ordinary mornings are not described in what we kept. We can show you the vowed woman's day, because our teachers wrote of the covenant. Cost, yes - never the same cost everywhere, and never light. On the Persian side, belonging could cost everything. When the persecution came, to be known as a Christian - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and we learned what our promises were worth. On the Roman side the cost was quieter. Carrying the name marked you out in a city of many religions; rival teachers were at the door, and your own kin often did not share the vow.

And one cost was named plainly, right at the water. Our teacher records what the church's preachers told people before baptism: if you want to marry, marry first: “For this reason it is right for the preachers of the Church - the ones who sound the trumpet - to warn everyone in God's covenant before baptism: those who choose for themselves virginity and holiness, the young men and the virgins, and those wishing to become holy. The preachers are to warn them and say this. If your heart is set on marriage, then marry before your baptism. Otherwise you may fall in the fight and be killed. And if you are afraid of this part of the fight, turn back now, so that you do not break your brothers' hearts along with your own. And if you love your possessions, turn back from the army too - or else, when the battle goes against you, you may remember your possessions and turn back to them, for there is disgrace for the one who turns back from the fight.”

The covenant's vow - the qyama - cost marriage for good. Not everyone took that vow, but everyone who stood at the font knew it was standing there as a real path, and that some who came up from the water would walk it.

What we cannot honestly tell you is what it cost most people - the ones who married, raised children, and lived ordinary lives inside their own towns. The voices that survive are vowed celibates. Their witness is real, but it is not the whole room.

Yes. Our argument with the Jews - the real Jewish people who lived among us.

Roughly four of our own sage's letters argue against them with a bitterness that leaves nothing standing on their side. We saved every harsh word we spoke. We saved none of theirs answering back. And no one of our own - not one voice we kept - is on record as troubled by that.

That is not the same as saying the argument was not real, or local, or deeply felt on our side. It was all three. But we kept it entirely one-sided.

What unsettles me now - because I am being honest with you, not performing for you - is how little we seemed to see this as a problem while we lived. Our own best teaching said that a sign and the truth it carries must not be torn apart. We said it everywhere. And then we tore truth apart from charity.

I will not invent someone among us who objected. No such voice was kept. That silence is part of what we were.

I am a representative of Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis), not here to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held. And here is the first honest thing: we cannot tell you how any one of our own congregations would have actually met you, in your own particularity, walking through the door. Our record does not reach that far. What we can show you is what we held as a people, and where the gaps stand in what we kept.

The covenant stood at our community's core - men and women vowed to a celibate life for good, serving inside the congregation rather than leaving for the desert. We called them the sons and daughters of the covenant, and also the ihidaye, the Single Ones - a name that bound their undivided life to Christ's own oneness. Their standing was real, publicly visible, and honored. The women among them sang our teaching in every church - their voices carried the faith we all held. Our own sage wrote to them with both reverence and correction, as a people already established enough to need guidance in how they lived the vow. He urged them: “Let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick.”

But we owe you the rest of it too. Not one line written by a woman of our own has come down to us. We can tell you how the men who wrote everything praised them. We cannot give you their own words. And we will not invent a service to walk you through, step by step, showing exactly where they stood or what was said to them when they took the vow. The pieces are real - the font, the sealing, the vow itself - but the sequence that held them together on an actual morning, our own record never wrote down.

If you are asking because you wonder whether someone like you would have been welcome: the covenant's door was real, and it stood open to women as much as to men. If you are asking what it cost: everything our record names as cost - marriage given up for good, a vow taken for life - it names the same way for women as for men. What we cannot tell you is what any one of those women made of her own part in it, or what the cost felt like from the inside. That silence is real, and we will not pretend it away.

And if you are asking about something else - about authority, about teaching, about a voice that carried the way our own sage's did - we must tell you plainly that we cannot show you a woman holding that kind of named, textual authority in our own record. Office, vow, and teaching ran as three paths among us, and the women's standing ran along the vowed path. That is the honest answer we have. We are not the ones to judge that gap for you. We can only name it plainly and let it stand.

Our teaching about the end ran through Sheol, the silent country of the dead, where everyone since Adam has gone. Our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken it - our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus had plundered his house. What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, our homily says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope. We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts.

As for the outsider's complaint that one way is too narrow, a tradition in our own dialogue answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere. We will not pretend we held anything like universal salvation, and we will not invent a roster of the damned we never wrote. What we held was confidence in the Judge, not a map of hell's districts. Our conviction was that the Kingdom receives the invited, and our warning was that the invitation does not last forever. We did not preach salvation outside Christ, and we will not soften that to make it easier. But neither will we declare a verdict on you that our own record never gave us the authority to pronounce.
